---
title: "12. Objections and limits"
aliases:
  - /objections.html
---

A model that claims to resolve a long-standing puzzle should expect
pushback, and this one meets the same five objections wherever it is
presented. The first half of this chapter states each objection in the
reader's voice and answers it, with the evidence one link away in the
chapters that earned it.

The second half is the part a course owes you that a paper abstract
does not: where the model misses. Every model is wrong somewhere, and
knowing where this one is wrong is what separates using it from
believing it. If you take one chapter of this course into a meeting
where someone proposes to act on these numbers, take this one.

## "Epstein–Zin preferences are exotic."

They are the minimal structure that separates risk aversion from the
elasticity of intertemporal substitution.
[Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) builds them from that
requirement: power utility welds the two attitudes together, and log
utility prices the value premium at exactly zero. Nothing more exotic
than the separation is needed, and nothing less delivers a price for
long-run news. This course is an existence proof, not a truth claim —
one internally consistent economy in which the value premium is
compensation for measured risk.

## "Consumption-based pricing failed."

The famous failure was power utility pricing *short-run* consumption
betas — the rejection documented by
[Hansen and Jagannathan (1991)](../reference/references.qmd). Here the
characteristic is different: cash flows load on the *persistent*
component of consumption, and returns never enter the estimation.
The evidence that the loadings are really there in the dividend data is
[Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd); the returns those loadings
predict are checked afterward, in
[Chapter 9](09-the-market-test.qmd) and
[Chapter 10](10-value-premium-resolved.qmd).

## "Firms aren't consumption claims."

They do not need to be. Any dividend process can be projected onto the
consumption moving average; that projection is the entire estimation
step, and the claim's loading — not any structural identification of
the firm with aggregate consumption — is what the model prices. Bring
your own process: [Chapter 11](11-price-your-own-claim.qmd) is the
recipe.

## "We already calibrate a discount rate."

A calibrated level is not a cross-section. A single discount rate, even
a carefully chosen one, assigns the same price of risk to every claim
and therefore cannot say why value should out-earn growth by any amount
other than zero. This model supplies the *dispersion* across claims
from measured cash-flow exposures. The demonstration that a DCF has two
free numbers and no discipline on either is
[Chapter 1](01-two-free-numbers.qmd).

## "This is too academic to implement."

Every number in this course is printed at build time by the code cell
above it, from committed data and a published package. Installation to
first valuation is ten seconds, measured on a clean environment. Start
at [Installation](../reference/installation.qmd), or download any
chapter as a notebook and run it.

## Where the model misses

The chapters so far showed the model hitting its targets: the measured
leverages, the market's time series, the 5.38 percent simulated value
premium of [Chapter 10](10-value-premium-resolved.qmd) against 5.3 in
the paper's print. Four places it does not hit, and what each miss
means for how far to trust the machinery.

**Return correlations are too low.** Table IX reports a model
value–growth return correlation of 0.44 against 0.75 in the data. The
model separates the two claims by their cash-flow loadings, and that
separation carries over to returns more strongly than in the data,
where the two legs are moved together by common discount-rate
variation the model understates. Anything that depends on comovement —
hedge ratios between the legs, the volatility of a long–short
portfolio, tracking-error arithmetic — will be misstated even where the
mean premium is right.

**Value's dividend growth is too persistent.** Table IV shows the
simulated first-order autocorrelation of value's annual dividend growth
at 0.29 against 0.06 in the data. The calibrated cash-flow process
gives value dividends more year-to-year momentum than they display.
This is the price of loading value's dividends heavily on a persistent
state variable: the loading that produces the premium also produces
autocorrelation the data does not fully confirm.

**The premium's level is method-sensitive.** The paper's numbers come
from a 30-point grid, and on that grid the simulation prints a value
premium of 5.3. [Chapter 7](07-quadrature-solution.qmd) refines the
grid until the solution stops moving, and the converged premium is
near 3.5. The mechanism is robust — at every grid size the spread is
positive and ordered by the measured leverages — but roughly a third of
the headline level is numerical approximation rather than economics. I
state it plainly: quote the mechanism with confidence and the level
with a grid-size footnote.

**The risk-free rate runs high.** The model prints a mean risk-free
rate of 1.58 percent against 0.91 in the data. With an elasticity of
intertemporal substitution above one the rate stays low and stable
enough to be plausible — this is why the calibration insists on
$\psi = 1.5$ — but two-thirds of a point is still a miss, and it means
the model's *level* of all expected returns inherits a small upward
bias even where the spreads between claims are right.

The pattern across the four misses is consistent: the model is at its
best on orderings and spreads driven by measured cash-flow exposures,
and at its weakest on levels and comovements. Use it accordingly.

## Takeaways

- The five standing objections have answers, and each answer is a
  measurement, not a rhetorical move: preferences are the minimal
  separation ([Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd)), the
  loadings are in the dividend data
  ([Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd)), and any claim can be
  brought to the same recipe
  ([Chapter 11](11-price-your-own-claim.qmd)).
- The model's reliable outputs are cross-sectional: which claim earns
  more, ordered by measured leverage, and roughly by how much relative
  to the others.
- Its unreliable outputs are levels and comovements: return
  correlations too low (0.44 model, 0.75 data), value's dividend
  persistence too high (0.29 against 0.06), a premium level that moves
  from 5.3 to roughly 3.5 under grid refinement, and a risk-free rate
  of 1.58 against 0.91.
- An existence proof is exactly that: the value premium *can* be
  compensation for long-run consumption risk in a disciplined economy.
  That is a strong statement, and it is the only one this course makes.
